---
title: "Save your work"
---

You have now run R code, created a summary table, and produced a figure inside your **`[DX]` notebook**.

Before ending your JupyterLab session, it is important to understand what is saved with the notebook and what remains temporary.

## 1. Save your `[DX]` notebook

Use the **Save** button in JupyterLab to save `getting-started.ipynb`.

We recommend saving regularly while you work.

Because this is a `[DX]` notebook, saving it stores the notebook persistently in your DNAnexus project.

::: {.callout-tip title="Save regularly"}
Do not wait until the end of an analysis to save your notebook.

Saving regularly gives you an up-to-date persistent record of your work in the DNAnexus project.
:::

## 2. What is saved with the notebook?

A saved `[DX]` notebook can preserve the content displayed inside it, including:

- your R code;
- text and notes;
- printed R output;
- tables;
- model summaries; and
- figures displayed below code cells.

For example, your `getting-started.ipynb` notebook should now contain both the code used to create the synthetic-data figure and the figure itself.

This makes the notebook a useful record of your analysis.

## 3. What is not saved by saving the notebook?

Saving the notebook does **not** preserve the live R session.

For example, earlier you created:

```r
dat <- read.csv(
  "/mnt/project/mcps-dnanexus-onboarding/data/example_data.csv"
)
```

The code that creates `dat` is saved in the notebook.

The object `dat` itself is held in the memory of the current R session and is temporary.

When this JupyterLab environment ends, that R session ends too.

The next time you start JupyterLab, you can recreate `dat` simply by running the relevant code again.

::: {.callout-note title="Notebook saved; R session temporary"}
A useful distinction is:

**Your `[DX]` notebook records how to create your analysis.**

**The R session contains the objects that currently exist while the analysis is running.**

Saving the notebook preserves the first, not the second.
:::

## 4. What about standalone files?

R can also create files outside the notebook.

For example:

```r
write.csv(
  dat,
  "example_output.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

If you run this code without specifying a persistent DNAnexus destination, the file is created in the **temporary JupyterLab computing environment**.

Saving the `[DX]` notebook does **not** automatically move that standalone file into your DNAnexus project.

The distinction is:

```text
[DX] notebook
│
├── R code                 → saved with notebook
├── displayed table        → saved with notebook
├── printed/model output   → saved with notebook
└── displayed figure       → saved with notebook

Temporary JupyterLab files
│
└── example_output.csv     → not automatically saved to project
```

::: {.callout-important title="Keep important files in the DNAnexus project"}
If you create a standalone file that you need to keep, it must be saved or moved into the persistent DNAnexus project.

For most exercises in this tutorial, you do not need to create standalone output files. Your `[DX]` notebook is the main record of your work.

We cover options for saving standalone outputs later in the tutorial.
:::

## 5. The notebook is your main analysis record

For many interactive analyses, keeping your:

- code;
- explanations;
- tables;
- model results; and
- figures

together in a `[DX]` notebook provides a simple and reproducible record of what you did.

You can still create standalone files when you need them, but you do not need to save every result as a separate file.

::: {.callout-tip title="Code is what makes your analysis reproducible"}
The most important thing to preserve is the **code needed to recreate your results**.

If your notebook contains the code needed to read the project data and reproduce your analysis, you can recreate temporary R objects in a new session.
:::

## 6. Save before you continue

Return to `getting-started.ipynb` and save it once more.

Before moving on, make sure you can still see:

- the R code you ran;
- the first rows of the synthetic dataset;
- the output from `dim()` and `summary()`;
- the summary table; and
- the figure.

On the next page, you will deliberately **terminate your JupyterLab environment**.

This will allow you to test that the notebook really is persistent.

## Checkpoint

Before continuing, confirm that:

- your notebook tab shows **`[DX]`**;
- your code and outputs are visible;
- you have saved the notebook; and
- you understand that the notebook is persistent but the current R session is temporary.

::: {.callout-success title="Ready"}
Your work is saved.

Next, you will safely end the temporary JupyterLab computing environment.
:::
